What fossils are and how they form:
A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of a living thing from a very long time ago, usually more than about 10,000 years. Fossils are found mostly in sedimentary rock, which forms in layers from sediments such as sand and mud.

Fossil formation needs quick burial after death, so scavengers, air and bacteria cannot destroy the body. Hard parts such as shells, bones and teeth fossilize best. Minerals carried by water fill spaces or replace the original material, and the sediment slowly becomes rock. Later, erosion and movement of the crust bring the fossil to the surface.

Most living things never become fossils. Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils.
Types of fossils:
Fossils have several types. Original remains are real bodies kept with little change, such as insects in amber or mammoths in ice. Petrified fossils have minerals replacing the original material, as in petrified wood.

A mold is a hollow shape left in rock after a body dissolves. A cast forms when a mold fills with minerals and hardens, so it copies the shape of the organism. A carbon film is a thin dark outline left by carbon, often from leaves.

Trace fossils show activity, not the body. Examples are footprints, burrows, nests, eggs and fossil droppings. They show how an animal lived and moved.
Uses of fossils and index fossils:
Fossils show how living things changed, which groups became extinct, and what past environments and climates were like. A marine fossil in a desert shows the area was once under the sea. Fossils also help find oil and gas.

In undisturbed sedimentary rock, lower layers are older. This gives relative age (older or younger). Radiometric dating gives age in years, using the half-life of radioactive atoms: after one half-life, half of the atoms remain.

An index fossil comes from an organism that lived a short time, spread over a wide area and was common. Finding the same index fossil in different places shows the rock layers have about the same age.
